cse-2023-cs-30.approach: Read the PDA as a counter: $s$ pushes one $A$ per $a$, $p$ pops one $A$ per $b$, and $q$ only empties the stack. Leaving for $q$ needs an $A$ still on top, which pins the counts down to $m \ge 1$ and $n < m$.
cse-2023-cs-30.given:
| From | To | Transitions |
|---|---|---|
| $s$ | $s$ | $a/\bot/A\bot$, $a/A/AA$ |
| $s$ | $p$ | $b/A/\epsilon$ |
| $p$ | $p$ | $b/A/\epsilon$ |
| $s$ | $q$ | $\epsilon/A/\epsilon$ |
| $p$ | $q$ | $\epsilon/A/\epsilon$ |
| $q$ | $q$ | $\epsilon/A/\epsilon$, $\epsilon/\bot/\epsilon$ |

Start in $s$ with stack $\bot$; accept by empty stack.

steps.title: What each state does
steps.body:
- In $s$, every $a$ pushes one $A$ ($a/\bot/A\bot$ and $a/A/AA$ keep what was on top and add an $A$).
- The first $b$ moves $s \to p$ and pops one $A$; in $p$ each further $b$ pops one $A$.
- $s \to q$ and $p \to q$ read nothing but **need $A$ on top** and pop it.
- Only $q$ can pop $\bot$, and nothing leaves $q$ or reads input there.

So the stack can become empty only in $q$, after all input is read, and the input must look like $a^m b^n$ ($a$'s in $s$, then $b$'s in $p$).

steps.title: At least one a is needed
steps.body:
Every move out of $s$ needs $A$ on top, and $A$ is pushed only by reading $a$. With no $a$ the PDA sits in $s$ with $\bot$ and is stuck, so $\epsilon$ and $b^n$ are rejected: $m \ge 1$.

After reading $a^m$ the stack is $\bot A^m$ (here $m = 2$: $\bot A A$).

steps.title: Each b cancels one A, and one A must survive
steps.body:
Each $b$ pops one $A$, so after $n$ $b$'s the stack is $\bot A^{m-n}$ (this needs $n \le m$).

To reach $q$ the PDA pops **one more** $A$ with $\epsilon/A/\epsilon$ (from $p$, or from $s$ when $n = 0$). That needs $m - n \ge 1$, i.e. $n < m$.

If $n = m$, the PDA is in $p$ with $\bot$ on top and $p$ has no move on $\bot$: stuck, rejected.

scene.caption: $b$ read: one $A$ popped, one left ($n = 1 < m = 2$).

steps.title: q empties the stack
steps.body:
In $q$, $\epsilon/A/\epsilon$ pops the remaining $m - n - 1$ $A$'s and $\epsilon/\bot/\epsilon$ pops $\bot$. Input consumed and stack empty, so the string is accepted.

Trace of $aab$ (stack written bottom → top): $(s, aab, \bot) \vdash (s, ab, \bot A) \vdash (s, b, \bot AA) \vdash (p, \epsilon, \bot A) \vdash (q, \epsilon, \bot) \vdash (q, \epsilon, \text{empty})$.

steps.title: Collect the conditions
steps.body:
Accepted exactly when the input is $a^m b^n$ with $m \ge 1$ and $n < m$:

$$L(P) = \{a^m b^n \mid 1 \le m \text{ and } n < m\}$$

which is option (A). For contrast, $ab$ ($n = m$) is rejected: after the $b$ the PDA is in $p$ with $\bot$ on top and has no move.

scene.caption: $ab$: stuck in $p$ with $\bot$ on top, so rejected.

answer.value: $\{a^m b^n \mid 1 \le m \text{ and } n < m\}$ — option (A)

optionAnalysis.reason: $m \ge 1$ is needed to leave $s$, and one $A$ must remain after the $b$'s for the $\epsilon/A/\epsilon$ move into $q$, so $n < m$.
Contains $ab$ ($n = m$) and $\epsilon$; both get stuck with $\bot$ on top outside $q$. This is the classic $a^n b^n$-style count, off by one.
$a^*b^*$ contains $b$, $abb$ and $\epsilon$, none of which is accepted; the PDA does compare the counts.
Contains $\epsilon$ and $b^n$ (rejected) and misses accepted strings with both letters such as $aab$.

cse-2023-cs-30.shortcut: Test $\epsilon$: the PDA starts in $s$ with $\bot$ and has no $\epsilon$-move on $\bot$ there, so $\epsilon$ is rejected. Options B, C and D all contain $\epsilon$ ($m = n = 0$), so only A survives.
pitfalls: Assuming acceptance by final state: there are no final states; the stack must be emptied, and only $q$ can pop $\bot$.
Treating it like the textbook $a^n b^n$ PDA: here the move into $q$ itself consumes an $A$, so one extra $a$ is required.
Forgetting the direct $s \to q$ edge, which accepts $a^m$ with $n = 0$ (e.g. $a$).
cse-2023-cs-30.verification: $a$ ($m = 1, n = 0$): push $A$, $\epsilon/A/\epsilon$ to $q$, pop $\bot$: accepted, and indeed $0 < 1$. $ab$ ($m = n = 1$): rejected, and $1 < 1$ is false. Both agree with option A.

cse-2023-cs-31.approach: Translate one loop iteration into bytes: multiplying by 8 is a left shift by 3, each `int` is 4 bytes so both array pointers advance by 4, and the loop must jump back to the exit test at `L01`.
cse-2023-cs-31.given: `int` is 32 bits; memory is byte-addressable. `r1` = `i`, `r2` = 10, `r3` → `a[i]`, `r4` → `b[i]`. Find `U1` (shift amount), `U2`/`U3` (pointer increments), `U4` (jump target).

steps.title: U1: multiply by 8 with a shift
steps.body:
`L02` loads `b[i]` into `r5`; `L03` must produce `b[i] * 8`. Since $8 = 2^3$,

$$x \times 8 = x \times 2^3 = x \ll 3,$$

so **U1 = 3**. A shift by 8 would multiply by $2^8 = 256$.

scene.code:
L01: jeq r1, r2, end
L02: lw  r5, 0(r4)
L03: shl r5, r5, 3
L04: sw  r5, 0(r3)
L05: add r3, r3, U2
L06: add r4, r4, U3
L07: add r1, r1, 1
L08: jmp U4
L09: end

steps.title: U2 and U3: advance by one int = 4 bytes
steps.body:
`a[i]` lives at $\text{base}_a + 4i$ because each `int` is $32/8 = 4$ bytes and addresses count bytes. After storing `a[i]`, `r3` must point to `a[i+1]` $= \text{base}_a + 4(i+1)$, i.e. `r3 + 4`. The same holds for `r4` and `b`.

So **U2 = 4** and **U3 = 4**. Adding 1 would point into the middle of the same `int`.

scene.code:
L01: jeq r1, r2, end
L02: lw  r5, 0(r4)
L03: shl r5, r5, 3
L04: sw  r5, 0(r3)
L05: add r3, r3, 4
L06: add r4, r4, 4
L07: add r1, r1, 1
L08: jmp U4
L09: end

steps.title: U4: jump back to the test
steps.body:
The C loop checks `i < 10` before **every** iteration. Here the check is `L01` (`jeq r1, r2, end` exits when `r1 = 10`). After `L07` increments `r1`, control must return to `L01`, so **U4 = L01**.

Jumping to `L02` would skip the test: the loop would never stop and would write past `a[9]`.

scene.code:
L01: jeq r1, r2, end
L02: lw  r5, 0(r4)
L03: shl r5, r5, 3
L04: sw  r5, 0(r3)
L05: add r3, r3, 4
L06: add r4, r4, 4
L07: add r1, r1, 1
L08: jmp L01
L09: end

steps.title: Check the whole loop
steps.body: With $(U1, U2, U3, U4) = (3, 4, 4, L01)$, iteration $i$ stores $8 \cdot b[i]$ into `a[i]` and moves both pointers 4 bytes. After 10 iterations `r1` $= 10 =$ `r2`, so `L01` exits, and `r3` $= \text{base}_a + 10 \times 4 = \text{base}_a + 40$, just past the 40-byte array. This is option (B).

optionAnalysis.reason: Shift by 8 multiplies by 256; `r4 + 1` misaligns `b`; jumping to `L02` skips the exit test.
$\ll 3$ is $\times 8$, both pointers advance by `sizeof(int)` = 4 bytes, and control returns to the loop test `L01`.
Shift by 8 ($\times 256$), 1-byte pointer steps and a jump that skips the test: three errors.
Shift and jump are right, but stepping by 1 byte treats `int` as 1 byte; addresses are byte addresses and `int` is 4 bytes.

cse-2023-cs-31.shortcut: $U1 = \log_2 8 = 3$ removes A and C; $U2 = \texttt{sizeof(int)} = 4$ removes D.
pitfalls: Writing the multiplier (8) instead of the shift count (3).
Incrementing a pointer by 1 element instead of by its size in bytes on a byte-addressable machine.
Looping back to the body (`L02`) instead of the condition (`L01`).
cse-2023-cs-31.verification: End state check: 10 iterations × 4 bytes = 40 bytes = size of `a[10]`, and the exit happens exactly when `r1` reaches `r2 = 10`, matching `for (i=0; i<10; i++)`.

animation.title: Loop body with the unknown operands

L01: jeq r1, r2, end
L02: lw  r5, 0(r4)
L03: shl r5, r5, U1
L04: sw  r5, 0(r3)
L05: add r3, r3, U2
L06: add r4, r4, U3
L07: add r1, r1, 1
L08: jmp U4
L09: end

cse-2023-cs-32.approach: Set the 10 Addr bits to 0 (start of a block); only the decoder inputs IA4 and IA3 remain, with place values $2^4 = 16$ and $2^3 = 8$. Read off the address that makes each decoder output active.
cse-2023-cs-32.given: 12-bit address IA11–IA0. Addr port (10 bits): IA11–IA5, IA2–IA0. Decoder: IA4 → A1, IA3 → A0; outputs Q0, Q1, Q2, Q3 → CS of X1, X2, X3, X4 (active high).

steps.title: Separate block-select bits from byte bits
steps.body:
The decoder sees $(A1, A0) = (IA4, IA3)$ and raises $Q_k$ for $k = 2 \cdot IA4 + IA3$. So block X$_{k+1}$ is selected when $(IA4, IA3)$ is the binary of $k$.

The other ten lines go to Addr. **Addr = 0** means all of IA11–IA5 and IA2–IA0 are 0.

steps.title: Starting address of each block
steps.body:
With every Addr bit 0, the address is $16 \cdot IA4 + 8 \cdot IA3$:

| Block | Output | IA4 IA3 | Address |
|---|---|---|---|
| X1 | Q0 | 00 | $0$ |
| X2 | Q1 | 01 | $8$ |
| X3 | Q2 | 10 | $16$ |
| X4 | Q3 | 11 | $16 + 8 = 24$ |

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body:
The starting locations are $(0, 8, 16, 24)$, option (C).

Because the select bits sit in the middle of the address, the blocks are interleaved in 8-byte chunks: 0–7 in X1, 8–15 in X2, 16–23 in X3, 24–31 in X4, then 32–39 in X1 again (IA5 = 1 is Addr = 8).

optionAnalysis.reason: $(0, 1, 2, 3)$ would need the decoder on IA1 IA0 (place values 2 and 1).
$(0, 1024, 2048, 3072)$ is the usual high-order decoding with IA11 IA10 on the decoder; here those lines go to Addr.
IA4 and IA3 have place values 16 and 8, so the blocks start at $0, 8, 16, 24$.
Exactly one CS is high for each address, so two blocks can never start at the same address.

cse-2023-cs-32.shortcut: Block $k$ ($k = 0..3$) starts at $k \times 2^3 = 8k$ because IA3 is the decoder's LSB.
pitfalls: Assuming the 1 KB blocks are contiguous (high-order decoding) without reading which lines feed the decoder.
Swapping A1 and A0: IA4 is the MSB input, so X3 (Q2) starts at 16, not 8.
cse-2023-cs-32.verification: Address 8 = 0000 0000 1000: IA3 = 1, IA4 = 0, so Q1 selects X2, and every Addr bit is 0, so it is X2's first byte. Address 7 is X1's Addr 7, so X1's first chunk ends just before 8.

cse-2023-cs-33.approach: Read each flip-flop's input from the figure, write next-state equations, and step from $(0,1,1)$ until a state repeats. The states on that cycle are the only ones that can ever appear.
cse-2023-cs-33.given: All three flip-flops share CLKIN. Inputs: $T_1 = \overline{Q_3}$, $D_2 = Q_1$, $T_3 = Q_2$. Start $(Q_1, Q_2, Q_3) = (0, 1, 1)$.

steps.title: Next-state equations
steps.body:
$$Q_1^+ = Q_1 \oplus \overline{Q_3}, \qquad Q_2^+ = Q_1, \qquad Q_3^+ = Q_3 \oplus Q_2$$

All flip-flops are clocked together, so every right-hand side uses the values **before** the clock edge.

steps.title: Clocks 4 to 7: back to the start
Find the state that never appears
steps.body:
Visited: $011, 000, 100, 010, 101, 111, 110$: seven of the eight 3-bit values. The missing one is $(0, 0, 1)$.

Options B $(1,0,0)$, C $(1,0,1)$ and D $(1,1,1)$ occur after clocks 2, 4 and 5. **Option (A)** can never be obtained.

scene.caption: $(0,0,1)$ is the only value missing from the cycle.

optionAnalysis.reason: $001$ is not on the 7-state cycle starting at $011$; it is a separate fixed point ($001 \to 001$).
$(1,0,0)$ is reached after the 2nd clock.
$(1,0,1)$ is reached after the 4th clock.
$(1,1,1)$ is reached after the 5th clock.

cse-2023-cs-33.shortcut: Apply the equations to $001$: $Q_1^+ = 0 \oplus 0 = 0$, $Q_2^+ = 0$, $Q_3^+ = 1 \oplus 0 = 1$, so $001 \to 001$. Its only predecessor is itself, so starting from $011$ the circuit can never enter it.
pitfalls: Missing the inverter: $T_1 = \overline{Q_3}$, not $Q_3$.
Updating the flip-flops one after another (using the new $Q_1$ to compute $Q_2^+$); they are clocked together.
Treating the D flip-flop like a T flip-flop: $Q_2^+ = Q_1$, not $Q_2 \oplus Q_1$.
cse-2023-cs-33.verification: The 8 states split into the 7-cycle $011 \to 000 \to 100 \to 010 \to 101 \to 111 \to 110 \to 011$ plus the self-loop $001$. Each of the 8 states has exactly one successor, which accounts for all of them.

cse-2023-cs-34.approach: Simplify $f$, then read the MUX tree as a truth table: M3 picks M1 when $B = 0$ and M2 when $B = 1$, and inside M1/M2 the input with index $2A + C$ is routed out. So each $X_i$ is just $f$ at the matching $(A, B, C)$.
cse-2023-cs-34.given: M1: inputs X0–X3, $S_1 = A$, $S_0 = C$. M2: inputs X4–X7, $S_1 = A$, $S_0 = C$. M3: input 0 = M1, input 1 = M2, $S = B$. Target: $f = \overline{A} + \overline{A}\,\overline{C} + A\overline{B}C$.

steps.title: Simplify the function
steps.body:
Absorption: $\overline{A} + \overline{A}\,\overline{C} = \overline{A}$. Then $\overline{A} + A\,Y = \overline{A} + Y$ with $Y = \overline{B}C$:

$$f = \overline{A} + A\overline{B}C = \overline{A} + \overline{B}C$$

steps.title: How the inputs are routed
steps.body:
M3 has $S = B$: output $=$ M1 when $B = 0$, M2 when $B = 1$. In M1 and M2, $S_1 S_0 = A\,C$ selects input number $2A + C$. Hence

$$X_{2A+C} = f(A, 0, C), \qquad X_{4 + 2A + C} = f(A, 1, C).$$

optionAnalysis.reason: $X_3 = 0$ drops the term $A\overline{B}C$ ($A=1, B=0, C=1$ gives $f = 1$), and $X_6 = 1$ is wrong ($A=1, B=1, C=0$ gives $f = 0$).
$X_3 = 0$ drops $A\overline{B}C$, and $X_7 = 1$ is wrong: $A=B=C=1$ gives $f = 0$.
Matches $f(A,0,C) = \overline{A} + C$ on M1 and $f(A,1,C) = \overline{A}$ on M2.
$X_0 = 0$ already fails: with $A = B = C = 0$ the term $\overline{A}$ makes $f = 1$. (D) also sets $X_6 = X_7 = 1$, although $f = 0$ whenever $A = B = 1$.

cse-2023-cs-34.shortcut: $f = 1$ whenever $A = 0$, so $X_0 = X_1 = X_4 = X_5 = 1$ (removes D). With $A = 1$, $f = \overline{B}C$ is 1 only for $B = 0, C = 1$, so among $X_2, X_3, X_6, X_7$ only $X_3 = 1$. Only C has that.
pitfalls: Swapping the select lines: $A$ drives $S_1$ (the MSB), so the index is $2A + C$, not $2C + A$.
Swapping M3's inputs: M1 feeds input 0 (taken when $B = 0$).
cse-2023-cs-34.verification: Spot checks through the circuit: $A=1, B=0, C=1$: M3 takes M1, index 3, $X_3 = 1$, and $f = 0 + 0 + 1 = 1$. $A=1, B=1, C=1$: M3 takes M2, index 3, $X_7 = 0$, and $f = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0$.

cse-2023-cs-35.approach: Decode P first: it is exactly $-16 = -2^4$. Multiplying by a power of two flips the sign and adds 4 to Q's biased exponent; Q's 23-bit fraction is copied unchanged.
concepts: Multiplying by a power of two

steps.title: Multiply sign, exponent and significand
steps.body:
- Sign: $1 \oplus 0 = 1$ (negative).
- Significand: $1.0 \times 1.f = 1.f$, already normalised, so the fraction is unchanged.
- Exponent: $2^4 \times 2^{-1} = 2^3$; biased $= 126 + 4 = 130 = 1000\,0010_2$.

$$P \times Q = -1.f \times 2^{3} \approx -13.76$$

optionAnalysis.reason: `0x404C2EF4` is positive (sign 0), has exponent 128 and a changed fraction ($100\,1100\ldots$). The product of a negative and a positive number is negative.
`0x405C2EF4` keeps the fraction but is positive with exponent 128, i.e. $+4Q$: wrong sign and wrong power of two.
Sign 1, exponent $126 + 4 = 130$, fraction of Q unchanged.
`0xC14C2EF4` has the right sign and exponent but the fraction starts $100\,1100$ instead of $101\,1100$; multiplying by $2^4$ never changes the fraction.

cse-2023-cs-35.shortcut: $\times(-16)$ means: add 4 to the exponent field, i.e. add $4 \times 2^{23} = \texttt{0x02000000}$, then set the sign bit: $\texttt{0x3F5C2EF4} + \texttt{0x02000000} = \texttt{0x415C2EF4}$, and with the sign bit set, $\texttt{0xC15C2EF4}$.
pitfalls: Adding the biased exponents ($131 + 126$) without subtracting the bias once.
Forgetting the sign: only options C and D are negative.
Reading the exponent from the first two hex digits: the exponent field straddles the nibble boundary (bits 30–23).
cse-2023-cs-35.verification: Decimal check: $1.f = 1 + \texttt{5C2EF4}/2^{23} = 1 + 6041332/8388608 \approx 1.7202$, so $Q \approx 0.8601$ and $P \times Q \approx -13.76$. Decoding C: $-1.7202 \times 2^{130-127} = -1.7202 \times 8 \approx -13.76$.

cse-2023-cs-36.approach: A max-heap is a complete binary tree of height $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$. EXTRACT-MAX sifts the moved last element down one root-to-leaf path and INSERT bubbles the new key up one leaf-to-root path, with $O(1)$ work per level.
concepts: Height of a complete binary tree

steps.title: Height of an n-element heap
steps.body:
A heap is a complete binary tree, so levels $0..h-1$ are full: $2^h \le n < 2^{h+1}$, which gives $h = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$. Each operation below moves an element along one path, so it does at most $h$ swaps.

Example heap: $[50, 30, 40, 10, 20, 35, 25]$, $n = 7$, $h = \lfloor \log_2 7 \rfloor = 2$.

steps.title: EXTRACT-MAX: sift-down, O(log n)
steps.body:
Reading the maximum (the root) is $O(1)$, but it must also be **deleted**: move the last element to the root, shrink the heap, and sift down. At each level compare with both children and swap with the larger one. That is at most $h$ swaps.

In the example: remove 50, move 25 to the root; $25 < 40$ swap; $25 < 35$ swap. That is 2 swaps $= h$, the worst case.

steps.title: INSERT: sift-up, O(log n)
steps.body:
Put the key in the next free leaf and swap it with its parent while it is larger. That is at most $h$ swaps; the worst case is a key larger than everything, which rises to the root.

In the example: insert 45 as the right child of 35; $45 > 35$ swap; $45 > 40$ swap. Two swaps $= h$.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Both operations are $O(\log n)$ in the worst case, option (B).

optionAnalysis.reason: Neither is $O(1)$ in the worst case: both may move an element through all $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ levels.
Each operation walks one root-leaf path of a tree of height $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.
EXTRACT-MAX must restore the heap ($O(\log n)$), and INSERT never needs $O(n)$: it only compares along one path.
Confuses EXTRACT-MAX with FIND-MAX (peek), which is $O(1)$; deleting the root needs a sift-down.

cse-2023-cs-36.shortcut: Only FIND-MAX is $O(1)$ in a binary heap; every operation that changes the heap (insert, delete, extract, increase-key) is $O(\log n)$.
pitfalls: Confusing *extract* (read and delete) with *peek*.
Quoting $O(n)$ for insert: $O(n)$ is BUILD-HEAP or searching for an arbitrary key, not insertion.
Using the average case (insert of a random key is $O(1)$ expected); the question asks for the worst case.
cse-2023-cs-36.verification: In the 7-element example both operations took exactly $2 = \lfloor \log_2 7 \rfloor$ swaps, and each swap moves the element one level, so no operation can exceed the height.

cse-2023-cs-37.approach: `foo` returns the sum of a subtree and prints it **after** both recursive calls, so it prints subtree sums in post-order. List the nodes in post-order and write each subtree sum.

steps.title: What foo prints, and when
steps.body:
`foo(NULL)` $= 0$, and otherwise `retval = val + foo(left) + foo(right)`, which is the sum of the subtree. The `printf` runs after both recursive calls, so the order is **left, right, node** (post-order).

Post-order of the tree: $3, 8, 5, 13, 11, 10$.

steps.title: Right subtree of 10
steps.body:
`foo(11)` first calls `foo(NULL)` $= 0$ (prints nothing), then

- `foo(13)` $= 13$, prints **13**
- `foo(11)` $= 11 + 0 + 13 = 24$, prints **24**

optionAnalysis.reason: Plain post-order of the node **values**; `foo` prints subtree sums, not `p->val`.
In-order of the values (sorted, since the tree is a BST); neither the order nor the values match.
Subtree sums in post-order: $3, 8, 16, 13, 24, 50$.
The right sums but in in-order (3, 16, 8, 50, 24, 13); the print happens after both calls, not between them.

cse-2023-cs-37.shortcut: The last number printed is the root's subtree sum, i.e. the sum of all nodes: $10 + 5 + 11 + 3 + 8 + 13 = 50$. Only C ends in 50, since D prints 50 in the middle.
pitfalls: Printing `p->val` instead of `retval`.
Placing the print between the calls (in-order) or before them (pre-order).
cse-2023-cs-37.verification: Every leaf prints its own value (3, 8, 13), each internal node prints its value plus its children's sums ($5+3+8=16$, $11+0+13=24$), and the root prints the grand total 50.

cse-2023-cs-38.approach: Build a separating permutation in independent stages and multiply (product rule): choose the $2k$ positions holding $A \cup B$, arrange the other $n - 2k$ elements, decide which set comes first, and order each set inside its block.

steps.title: Positions of A ∪ B
steps.body: Choose which $2k$ of the $n$ positions hold the elements of $A \cup B$: $\binom{n}{2k}$ ways. In a separating permutation the first $k$ of these positions hold one set and the last $k$ hold the other.

steps.title: The other n − 2k elements
steps.body: The remaining $n - 2k$ elements fill the remaining positions in any order: $(n - 2k)!$ ways.

steps.title: Which set goes first
steps.body: Either all of $A$ precedes all of $B$, or all of $B$ precedes all of $A$: 2 ways. Since $k \ge 1$, both cannot hold at once, so the two cases do not overlap.

steps.title: Order inside each block
steps.body: The $k$ elements of $A$ can be ordered in $k!$ ways within their block, and likewise $k!$ for $B$: $(k!)^2$.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body:
$$\binom{n}{2k}\,(n-2k)! \times 2 \times (k!)^2 = 2\binom{n}{2k}(n-2k)!\,(k!)^2$$

which is option (D).

optionAnalysis.reason: $n!$ counts every permutation; for $k \ge 2$ many do not separate, e.g. $a_1 b_1 a_2 b_2 \ldots$.
Places the other elements but forgets the internal orders $(k!)^2$ of $A$ and $B$ and the factor 2.
Counts only the case "$A$ before $B$"; the factor 2 for "$B$ before $A$" is missing.
Positions $\binom{n}{2k}$, others $(n-2k)!$, which set first $2$, internal orders $(k!)^2$.

cse-2023-cs-38.shortcut: Symmetry: the relative order of the $2k$ elements of $A \cup B$ is uniform over $(2k)!$ orders, of which $2(k!)^2$ separate. Count $= n! \cdot \frac{2(k!)^2}{(2k)!} = 2\binom{n}{2k}(n-2k)!\,(k!)^2$, since $\frac{n!}{(2k)!} = \binom{n}{2k}(n-2k)!$.
pitfalls: Reading "one of the following is true" as only the first bullet (losing the factor 2).
Forgetting that the elements inside $A$ (and inside $B$) can be permuted.
cse-2023-cs-38.verification: Small case $n = 4$, $k = 2$, $A = \{1,2\}$, $B = \{3,4\}$: separating permutations are $12\,34$, $21\,34$, $12\,43$, $21\,43$ and the 4 with $B$ first, giving 8. Formula: $2 \cdot \binom{4}{4} \cdot 0! \cdot (2!)^2 = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 4 = 8$.

cse-2023-cs-39.approach: Check each property straight from the definition of $\sim$: equal classes force equal $f$-values (well-defined), $f$ onto gives $F$ onto, and equal $F$-values force equal classes (one-to-one).

steps.title: F is well-defined
steps.body: A class can be named by any of its members, so $F$ must not depend on the representative. If $[x] = [y]$ then $x \sim y$, i.e. $f(x) = f(y)$, so $F([x]) = f(x) = f(y) = F([y])$. Hence $F$ is well-defined and **(A) is false**.

scene.caption: Example: 1 and 2 share the image p, so they form one class.

steps.title: F is onto
steps.body: Take any $b \in B$. Since $f$ is onto, some $a \in A$ has $f(a) = b$, and then $F([a]) = f(a) = b$. So **(B) is true**.

scene.caption: Every element of B is hit.

steps.title: F is one-to-one
steps.body: Suppose $F([x]) = F([y])$. Then $f(x) = f(y)$, which by definition means $x \sim y$, so $[x] = [y]$. So **(C) is true**, even though $f$ itself need not be one-to-one.

steps.title: Bijective
steps.body: One-to-one and onto, so $F$ is a bijection $\mathcal{E} \to B$: **(D) is true**. Answer: **B, C, D**.

optionAnalysis.reason: $F$ is well-defined: members of one class have the same $f$-value by the very definition of $\sim$.
Every $b \in B$ equals $f(a)$ for some $a$, hence equals $F([a])$.
$F([x]) = F([y]) \Rightarrow f(x) = f(y) \Rightarrow x \sim y \Rightarrow [x] = [y]$.
Onto (B) and one-to-one (C) together make $F$ a bijection.

cse-2023-cs-39.shortcut: Grouping $A$ into the fibres $f^{-1}(b)$ of a surjection gives exactly one class per $b \in B$, so $\lvert \mathcal{E} \rvert = \lvert B \rvert$ and $F$ matches them one to one.
pitfalls: Thinking $F$ inherits the non-injectivity of $f$: collapsing each fibre to one class removes it.
Ticking A because $F$ is defined via a representative; it is well-defined precisely because $\sim$ is defined by $f$.
cse-2023-cs-39.verification: Example $f$: $1, 2 \mapsto p$, $3 \mapsto q$, $4, 5 \mapsto r$. Classes $\{1,2\}, \{3\}, \{4,5\}$ map to $p, q, r$: three classes, three images, each hit once.

animation.title: Example: A → classes → B
animation.caption: Example: elements of A (left), classes in ℰ (middle), B (right).

cse-2023-cs-40.approach: A byte-stream protocol numbers bytes, and a sequence number must not be reused while an old segment carrying it can still be alive, i.e. within one maximum segment lifetime. So $2^{n}$ must be at least the number of bytes that can be sent in one MSL.
cse-2023-cs-40.given: Bandwidth $100$ Mbps, RTT $150$ ms, MSL $= 2$ min $= 120$ s. Sequence numbers count bytes.

steps.title: Bytes that can be sent in one MSL
steps.body:
$$100 \text{ Mbps} = \frac{100 \times 10^6}{8} = 1.25 \times 10^7 \text{ bytes/s}$$

$$1.25 \times 10^7 \times 120 = 1.5 \times 10^9 \text{ bytes}$$

All of these need distinct sequence numbers.

steps.title: Check each option by wrap-around time
steps.body:
Wrap time $= 2^n / (1.25 \times 10^7)$ s, which must be at least $120$ s:

| Bits | $2^n$ | Wrap time | Valid? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 30 | $1\,073\,741\,824$ | $\approx 85.9$ s | no |
| 32 | $4\,294\,967\,296$ | $\approx 343.6$ s | yes |
| 34 | $17\,179\,869\,184$ | $\approx 1374.4$ s | yes |
| 36 | $68\,719\,476\,736$ | $\approx 5497.6$ s | yes |

The RTT (150 ms) does not matter here; it sizes the window (bandwidth × RTT), not the sequence space. Answer: **B, C, D**.

optionAnalysis.reason: $2^{30}$ bytes are sent in about 85.9 s < 120 s MSL, so numbers would wrap while old duplicates may still be alive.
$2^{32}$ bytes take about 343.6 s ≥ 120 s to wrap.
$2^{34}$ bytes take about 1374 s to wrap, comfortably above the MSL.
$2^{36}$ bytes take about 5498 s to wrap; longer fields are always safe.

cse-2023-cs-40.shortcut: $\log_2(1.5 \times 10^9) = \log_2 1.5 + 9\log_2 10 \approx 0.585 + 29.9 = 30.48$, so at least 31 bits; every option from 32 bits up works.
pitfalls: Counting bits instead of bytes ($10^8 \times 120 = 1.2 \times 10^{10}$ would demand 34 bits and wrongly reject 32).
Using the RTT in place of the MSL: wrap-around safety is about how long old segments survive, not the RTT.
Counting segments instead of bytes: in a byte stream every byte gets a number.
cse-2023-cs-40.verification: Real TCP uses 32-bit byte sequence numbers; at 100 Mbps that is safe for about 343 s, more than the 120 s MSL, consistent with 32 bits being valid and 30 bits not.

cse-2023-cs-41.approach: Check the group axioms for symmetric difference: closure, associativity (Δ is XOR of membership), identity $\emptyset$, and inverses, where $A \Delta A = \emptyset$ makes every set its own inverse.

steps.title: Closure and associativity
steps.body:
$A \Delta B \subseteq X$, so it is again in $2^X$ (closure).

An element $x$ is in $A \Delta B$ iff it lies in **exactly one** of $A, B$, i.e. its membership bits XOR to 1. XOR is associative, so $(A \Delta B) \Delta C$ and $A \Delta (B \Delta C)$ are both the set of elements lying in an odd number of $A, B, C$. So $\Delta$ is associative.

steps.title: Identity: the empty set
steps.body:
$$A \Delta \emptyset = (A - \emptyset) \cup (\emptyset - A) = A \cup \emptyset = A$$

and $\emptyset \Delta A = A$ likewise, so $e = \emptyset$.

steps.title: Inverse: every set is its own
steps.body:
$$A \Delta A = (A - A) \cup (A - A) = \emptyset = e$$

so $A^{-1} = A$: **(D) is true**. The complement does not work: $A \Delta \overline{A} = A \cup \overline{A} = X \neq \emptyset$ whenever $X$ is nonempty, so **(C) is false**.

scene.caption: Diagonal is all ∅: each set is its own inverse.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Closure, associativity, identity and inverses all hold, so $H$ is a group (indeed abelian, since $\Delta$ is symmetric): **(A) is true**, which makes **(B) false**. Answer: **A, D**.

optionAnalysis.reason: $\Delta$ is closed and associative, $\emptyset$ is the identity, and every element has an inverse.
Its first half is true, but $H$ *is* a group, so the statement is false.
$A \Delta \overline{A} = X$, not the identity $\emptyset$ (for nonempty $X$). The complement would be the inverse only if $X$ were the identity.
$A \Delta A = \emptyset$, the identity.

cse-2023-cs-41.shortcut: Identify each subset with its characteristic bit-vector: $\Delta$ becomes bitwise XOR on $\{0,1\}^{\lvert X \rvert}$, a group in which $0$ is the identity and every vector is its own inverse.
pitfalls: Taking $X$ as the identity (that is the identity for $\cap$, not $\Delta$), which leads to option C.
Doubting associativity because $\Delta$ is defined with set differences; the XOR view settles it.
cse-2023-cs-41.verification: For $X = \{1, 2\}$ the Cayley table of $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{1,2\}\}$ is a Latin square with $\emptyset$ on the diagonal: the Klein four-group.

cse-2023-cs-42.approach: Add three delays: iterative DNS (one RTT per tier: root, TLD, authoritative), then the TCP handshake plus the HTML request, then the 10 objects. Non-persistent connections cost 2 RTT per batch of 5 objects; one persistent pipelined connection fetches all 10 in 1 RTT.
cse-2023-cs-42.given: DNS: 3 tiers, iterative, nothing cached, RTT to each server. Web server RTT also 1 RTT. HTML + 10 small objects (transmission time negligible).

steps.title: DNS: 3 RTT
steps.body: The local DNS server is on the local host and works iteratively: query root (1 RTT) → referral to the TLD server (1 RTT) → referral to the authoritative server (1 RTT), which returns the IP address. Total **3 RTT**.

steps.title: Base HTML file: 2 RTT
steps.body: TCP handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK takes **1 RTT**; the final ACK carries the HTTP GET, and the HTML comes back after **1 RTT**. Elapsed so far: $3 + 2 = 5$ RTT.

steps.title: Non-persistent HTTP, 5 parallel connections
steps.body:
Every object needs its own TCP connection: handshake (1 RTT) + request/response (1 RTT) $= 2$ RTT per batch. With 5 in parallel, the 10 objects need $10 / 5 = 2$ batches, so $2 \times 2 = 4$ RTT.

$$3 + 2 + 4 = 9 \text{ RTT}$$

So **(C) is correct** and (A) is not.

steps.title: Persistent HTTP with pipelining
steps.body:
The connection used for the HTML stays open. The browser sends all 10 GETs back-to-back and the 10 small objects return within **1 RTT**:

$$3 + 2 + 1 = 6 \text{ RTT}$$

So **(D) is correct** and (B) is not. Answer: **C, D**.

answer.value: **C, D** (9 RTT non-persistent with 5 parallel connections; 6 RTT persistent with pipelining)

optionAnalysis.reason: 7 RTT counts only 1 RTT per object batch, forgetting that non-persistent HTTP opens a new TCP connection (one more RTT) for every object.
5 RTT is the time to get just the HTML (3 DNS + 2); the pipelined objects still need 1 more RTT.
$3$ (DNS) $+ 2$ (HTML) $+ 2 \times 2$ (two batches of 5 non-persistent fetches) $= 9$ RTT.
$3$ (DNS) $+ 2$ (HTML) $+ 1$ (all 10 objects pipelined) $= 6$ RTT.

cse-2023-cs-42.shortcut: Common part = 3 (DNS) + 2 (HTML) = 5 RTT. Then add $2\lceil 10/5 \rceil = 4$ for non-persistent parallel, or $1$ for persistent pipelined.
pitfalls: Counting DNS as 1 RTT: an iterative lookup over 3 tiers with empty caches needs 3 round trips.
Forgetting the TCP handshake before the first GET.
Reusing connections in the non-persistent case: each object needs a fresh handshake.
cse-2023-cs-42.verification: The two answers differ by exactly the object phase: non-persistent spends $4$ RTT (2 batches × 2) where pipelined spends $1$, and $9 - 6 = 4 - 1 = 3$.
